siteSource.note: Paths are repo paths at this commit, read from the read-only local clone C:/Users/kygs/teaching-app-fix at the same commit (not modified). SHA256 values recomputed from the clone on 18 November 2026 and match the crosswalk inventory. Investment and loans lessons 03, 05, 06, 07, 11, 14 and 15 use data-step-id sections. Lessons 01 and 02 are retired duplicates of 05 and 06 and are not used; lesson04 (an exam-practice page) is not used.

recommendations: Run i01 to i11 in outline order. Standard 2 students take all eleven. Standard 1 students take i01, i02, i03, i05, i08, i09, i10 and i11 (i04, i06 and i07 are Standard 2 only); in i08 the shares row is marked Standard 2.

Joins: i01 opens on math-s12-a13's final frame (the coin jar beside empty axes), which matches a08's right panel, so both courses arrive at the same picture. i05 and i08 must stand without i04, i06 and i07, because Standard 1 viewers arrive from i03 and i05.

Pace flags (gentler Standard pace): i02 is likely to need a split into i02a (future value) and i02b (present value and the rate); i04 and i06 are at risk and have suggested splits; i08 and i10 should be watched (i10 runs long only if the site's rate-finding example is kept).

Notation: use the syllabus letters on screen, FV = PV(1 + r)^n, I = Prn, S = V_0 - Dn and S = V_0(1 - r)^n. Site lessons 05 and 06 write A = P(1 + rn) and A = P(1 + r)^n; lesson11 already uses FV = PV(1 + r)^n.

Beyond the syllabus on the site, kept out of the videos: effective annual rate (lesson06 card 07, lesson07), flat-rate loan true rates and the Rule of 72 with logarithms (lesson07), superannuation, ETF and tax modelling (lesson11 we-2, SA 2, SA 3).

Money figures (root ruling 5): RBA cash rate 4.85% from 3 November 2026; ABS CPI 4.3% in the year to September 2026; top 12-month term deposits about 5.5% to 5.7% p.a. and bonus savings rates about 5.5% to 6.5% p.a. in November 2026; 2026-27 NSW transfer duty table (Revenue NSW); a major broker's current tiers ($5 to $29.95 flat, 0.12% above $25 000); ATO diminishing value rate for cars 25% (200% of an 8-year effective life). Sources are listed in each pack. Each video says once that rates and fees change.

New site findings are logged as MS-11 to MS-18 in docs/production/claude-pm/site-corrections-maths-standard.md (section 5): three compound-interest rounding errors in lesson06 (MS-11 to MS-13), a wrong answer in lesson07 (MS-14), a rounding slip and a dated super figure in lesson11 (MS-15, MS-16) and two copy problems in lesson03 (MS-17, MS-18), followed by four teaching gaps (present value and rate, inflation as compound growth, appreciation, graph comparisons with digital tools) and two structure notes.

Kit needs for i01 to i11 are in docs/production/claude-pm/checks/maths-standard-kit-needs-i.md; the main new parts are a share table and an interest-block stack, plus SpreadsheetGrid from the a-strand list.

entryKnowledge.text: Simple interest: interest on the principal only, a straight-line graph.
An exponential model y = k a^x with a = 1 + r (Standard 2; Standard 1 met y = a^x tables in a05).
cib256693a: a 5% increase multiplies by 1.05.

entries.startBoundary: i01's interest was paid out, so the balance stayed at the principal. Leave the interest in the account instead, and next year's interest is worked out on a bigger balance.
entries.stopBoundary: Compound interest as interest added to the balance and then earning interest itself; year-by-year multiplying by (1 + r) (site card 05: $2000 at 5% for 3 years) leading to FV = PV(1 + r)^n with r and n per compounding period (syllabus letters); interest = FV − PV; present value as the amount to invest now, PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n; the interest rate per period from PV, FV and n by working backwards (calculator root or trial, Standard 2 and Standard 1 both require it). Effect of changing the compounding period and the per-period rate r ÷ 12 is i04; inflation and appreciation are i03; the simple-versus-compound graph comparison is i05.
entries.recommendation: Pace flag: future value, present value and the interest rate are three calculations, and the site teaches only the first (no PV or rate example; logged as a site gap). Likely split for a gentler pace: i02a (interest on interest; FV) and i02b (working backwards: PV and the rate). Use FV and PV on screen (syllabus), not the site's A and P. Effective annual rate (site card 07) is beyond the 2024 syllabus: leave it out.

entryKnowledge.text: FV = PV(1 + r)^n for an investment.
cib256693a: percentage increase.

entries.startBoundary: i02's formula grew money in a bank. The same multiply-every-year pattern also grows prices (inflation) and the value of things people own (appreciation).
entries.stopBoundary: Inflation as prices rising by a percentage each year, so a future price is FV = PV(1 + r)^n with r the inflation rate; what a dollar buys falls as prices rise; appreciation as an asset's value rising by a percentage each year (property, a collectable instrument), worked with the same formula; finding a past price or value by working backwards (PV) where useful; a short real-return comparison (an investment earning less than inflation loses buying power) without relying on the subtraction rule as exact. Depreciation (the falling direction) is i09 to i11.
entries.recommendation: Site gap: the site has no inflation-as-compound-growth example and no appreciation at all (crosswalk partial; logged). Teach both from the syllabus with original, sourced 2026 figures (ABS CPI 4.3% in the year to September 2026); keep lesson11's real-return numbers only as a brief contrast. Pace: not at risk.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do the rate, the term and the compounding period change an investment?

syllabusActions.text: Examine the effect of varying the interest rate, the term or the compounding period on the future value of an investment, with and without using digital tools
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Examine the effect of varying the interest rate, the term or the compounding period on the future value of an investment, with and without using digital tools

entryKnowledge.text: FV = PV(1 + r)^n, per-period r and n.
The same formula for prices and values.

entries.startBoundary: i02 and i03 compounded once a year. Banks also compound monthly or quarterly, and offer different rates and terms. Change one thing at a time and watch the future value.
entries.stopBoundary: Change one input at a time with the rest fixed: a higher rate gives a higher FV; a longer term gives a higher FV and the extra grows faster than the time (doubling the term more than doubles the interest); more frequent compounding with the same annual rate gives a slightly higher FV, using r ÷ k per period and n × k periods (k = 12 monthly, 4 quarterly, 2 half-yearly); by hand and with a digital tool (a spreadsheet or calculator app with one input changed). Effective annual rate, flat-rate loans and the Rule of 72 (site lesson07) are beyond the 2024 Standard syllabus and are not taught.
entries.recommendation: Use lesson06's numbers (card 06: $8000 at 4.8% half-yearly for 4 years; we-1 $10 000 at 8% quarterly; we-2 $5000 at 6% monthly, correct value $5983.40, not the site's $5983.50; drill 2(b) annual against monthly over 20 years). Pace flag: three variables plus the per-period conversion and a digital tool; watch, and split into i04a (rate and term) and i04b (compounding period) only if the design passes 570 s.

entries.startBoundary: Same principal, same rate, two accounts: one pays the interest out (i01), one leaves it in (i02). Put them side by side, year after year.
entries.stopBoundary: Compare simple and compound growth numerically (a year-by-year table) and graphically: simple interest graphs are straight lines (the same interest each year, linear) and compound interest graphs are curves that bend upward (exponential, interest on interest); both start at the principal and agree after one year, then compound pulls ahead; build the comparison in a spreadsheet (year column filled down, =P+P*r*n and =P*(1+r)^n, then a line graph); use a given graph to compare. Standard 1 compares numerically or from a given graph and uses the spreadsheet.

entries.startBoundary: Bank accounts grow at a rate set in advance. A share is different: it is a small part-ownership of a company, and its price moves every day.
entries.stopBoundary: A share as part-ownership of a company; two separate returns: the price changing (only banked when sold) and dividends (cash paid per share, quoted in cents); risk named plainly: prices can fall below what was paid and dividends can be cut, nothing is guaranteed; reading a share table row (Last, Change, High, Low, Div, Yield); dividend paid = number of shares × dividend per share; dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ current price × 100% (no franking); graphing a share price over time by hand and with a spreadsheet or app, and describing the trend, the highest and lowest points and the falls inside a rise; percentage change from the first price. Brokerage is i07.
entries.recommendation: Mirror lesson14's numbers exactly (Brindle Ltd row: $44.60, 162c, 3.63%; Kalina: 850 shares, 24c, $6.40, $204.00 and 3.75%; we-3 prices $3.20 to $3.95, 23.44%; the hook: 30c at $6.00 then $7.50, yield 5% then 4%). Invented company names only. No gambling framing: shares are investments with real risk. The site shows no digital-tool graph (cie1731909 "with and without using digital tools"); add a spreadsheet chart. Pace flag: three points; split into i06a (dividends and yield from a share table) and i06b (share price graphs over time) only if the design passes 570 s.

cib256693a: a percentage of an amount.

entries.startBoundary: i06 read the price on the screen. Buying at that price costs more, because a broker charges a fee on every trade.
entries.stopBoundary: Brokerage as the broker's fee on each trade; trade value = number of shares × price; a flat fee, a percentage of the trade value, or "the greater of" the two (work out both, take the larger); total cost of buying = trade value + brokerage; brokerage as a percentage of the trade value (why a fee matters more on a small parcel); the trade value where the two rules cost the same (site hook, $29 950); one short round trip (selling subtracts the fee) as the reason a price rise must first cover two fees. Comparing investment types is i08.
entries.recommendation: Keep lesson15's numbers exactly (Nadia, Theo, Sam; $29 950). The site's fees ($19.95, $29.95, 0.10% to 0.12%) match a major Australian broker's current tiers; say once that fees vary and change. The syllabus point is about purchasing; keep selling to one round-trip beat. Pace: not at risk.

One-sentence depreciation preview (root ruling 12; Standard 2 only).

entries.startBoundary: Investments grow. Most things a worker or a business buys do the opposite: tools, gear and vehicles lose value as they are used.
entries.stopBoundary: Depreciation as the loss in value of an asset over time; straight-line depreciation S = V_0 − Dn (syllabus letters): the same dollar amount D lost each period, so the graph is a straight line falling from V_0 with gradient −D (simple interest in reverse); find S after n years; find D from the start and end values, D = (V_0 − S) ÷ n; find when the value first falls below a level and round up to whole years (site we-1); salvage value means the modelled value, not a guaranteed sale price. Declining balance is i10; comparing the methods and the spreadsheet is i11.
entries.recommendation: Teaches depreciation fully (root ruling 12: a06 only previewed it). Keep lesson03's numbers (card: $24 000 losing $3000 a year; we-1: $85 000 losing $7400 a year, $40 600 after 6 years, below $30 000 after 8 complete years; drills). Pace: not at risk.

syllabusActions.text: Explain the similarities and differences between the declining balance formula and the compound interest formula
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Explain the similarities and differences between the declining balance formula and the compound interest formula

entryKnowledge.text: Straight-line depreciation, S = V_0 − Dn.
FV = PV(1 + r)^n.
Decay as multiplying by 1 − r each step (Standard 2).

entries.startBoundary: i09 took the same dollars off every year. A new car does not lose $6000 a year for ever: it loses a percentage of whatever it is worth now.
entries.stopBoundary: Declining-balance depreciation S = V_0(1 − r)^n: the same percentage of the current value lost each period, so the dollar loss shrinks every year and the graph is a decay curve that never reaches zero in the model; the multiplier 1 − r (18% gives 0.82); total depreciation = V_0 − S, never r × n × V_0; similarities with compound interest (same structure, a power of n, the same calculator steps) and differences (1 − r against 1 + r; value falls, the dollar change shrinks rather than grows). Finding r from two values is optional practice, not required by the syllabus wording. Comparing with straight-line is i11.
entries.recommendation: Keep lesson03's numbers ($32 000 at 18% for 4 years, $14 467.90, the site rounds to $14 468; we-2 $38 500 at 22% for 3 years, $18 270.25 and $20 229.75). The compound-interest comparison is a Standard 1 point (cid65c76c0); give it its own scene. A real anchor: the ATO's diminishing value rate for a car is 200% ÷ 8-year effective life = 25%. Pace flag: if we-4 (finding the rate with a fourth root) is kept, the video runs long; move it to a practice question or leave it out.
